newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee convertibility timetable ambitious-analysts. [corrected 15:45 gmt]
newsitem.headline: India rupee convertibility timetable ambitious-analysts. [corrected 15:45 gmt]

text.p: Making the Indian rupee fully convertible by the end of the century is a tall order bankers and economists said on Tuesday after the release of an official report mapping out a route to freeing the exchange rate.

A committee appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) submitted its recommendations, listing various preconditions needed before the rupee can be made convertible on the capital account (Corrects from current account).

Those conditions include an average inflation rate of three to five percent for the three year period until 2000, and a reduction in the fiscal deficit to GDP ratio to 3.5 percent by financial year 1999/2000,
"These are very difficult numbers to achieve going by our past record," Subir Biswas, senior treasurer at ABN-AMRO Bank said.
"It might take more time than three years," he said.
While there were reservations about the speed at which the rupee's value can be put in the lap of the markets, there was praise for the committee's approach.
"In terms of direction, it (the recommendations) are good," R. Balakrishnan, president of Dil Vikas Finance said. "but whether we can achieve the conditions is a matter of concern."
Analysts pointed out that Indian inflation rate had averaged at 6.0-7.0 percent and seldom fallen below 5.0 percent.
The fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP has been over 5.0 percent, although the government has targeted reducing it to 4.5 percent in 1997/98 fiscal year (April-March).
The panel also said a total deregulation of interest rate should precede full convertibility on the capital account, adding that it should take place this year and next.
"If the targets are met, we will achieve G7 status," one bank treasurer commented, reflecting the ambitious goals.

A decision on the recommendations will have to be taken by the finance ministry and some of the changes, like amendment of the RBI Act, giving the central bank more independence, will require parliament approval, analysts said.
The committe argued that the Act should be amended to allow the central bank a freer hand in pursuing inflation targets.
"Its recommendations like allowing Indian residents to invest in overseas markets may face political barriers, delaying the whole process," Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets said.
The left parties, especially communists, in the coalition have been opposing free market policies of the ruling United Front government.
A forex dealer at a European bank in Bombay said Indian economy was not strucutrally prepared for full convertibility.
"I don't see full convertibility in three to five years," he said. He said the absence of a deep and liquid money market and absence of term money market were a hindrance.
"Even our reserves are not enough for full convertibility," he said. India's forex reserves are close to $28 billion, compared to annual Indian imports of about $35 billion.
"The market was not expecting any bold or immediate steps," said an official of an American bank in Bombay.
He said the recent battering some of the south-east Asian currencies, like Thai baht, have taken may have led the Indian panel to take a cautious approach.
The committee's report stressed the need for a constant review of progress towards the various pre-conditions and the said flexibility in policy was required.
Analysts said full convertibility in the current scenario would only aggravate the central bank's dilemma in trying to arrest the rupee's rise by buying dollars from the market.
The RBI has been buying dollars to prevent the rupee's rise but the consequent injection of excess liquidity into the domestic money supply has worried the central bank, analysts said.
The rupee was quoted around 35.78 to the dollar on Tuesday.
"There is no great urgency for full convertibility," said another banker.
